title: Tammer v. Estonia
facts:
The applicant, Mr Enno Tammer, was at the material time a journalist and editor of the Estonian daily newspaper Postimees. On 3 April 1996 Postimees published an interview he conducted with another journalist, Mr Ülo Russak, entitled "Ülo Russak denies theft". It was prompted by an allegation by Ms Vilja Laanaru that Mr Russak, who had helped her write her memoirs, had published them without her consent.

Ms Laanaru is married to the Estonian politician Edgar Savisaar. In 1990, when Mr Savisaar was still married to his first wife, he became Prime Minister; Ms Laanaru, already working for him, became his assistant and continued to work with him, and in 1995, when he was Minister of the Interior, she was one of his counsellors. She had been politically active in the Centre Party led by Mr Savisaar and was an editor of the party's paper. In or around 1989 she gave birth to a child by Mr Savisaar; unwilling to place the child in a kindergarten, she entrusted the child to her parents. On 10 October 1995 Mr Savisaar was forced to resign as Minister of the Interior after the discovery of secret tape recordings of his conversations with other politicians; the same day Ms Laanaru issued a statement claiming full responsibility for the recordings. She then left the Ministry and began writing her memoirs with Mr Russak's help. In them she conceded that her statement of 10 October 1995 was untrue; according to Mr Russak, she also reflected on her relationship with Mr Savisaar, a married man, asking whether she had broken up his family, admitted she had not been as good a mother as she wished, and wondered whether she had paid too high a price in sacrificing her child to her career.

A dispute arose between her and Mr Russak over publication and authorship. Ms Laanaru brought a civil action before the Tallinn City Court, which on 29 March 1996 prohibited Mr Russak from publishing the manuscript pending resolution of the authorship issue. Mr Russak then published the material in the form of the information Ms Laanaru had given him; his account began appearing in Eesti Päevaleht on 1 April 1996. Later in 1996 Ms Laanaru published her own memoirs, stating that some of the information in Mr Russak's account was incorrect, without specifying in what respect.

In the interview of 3 April 1996 the applicant asked Mr Russak, inter alia:
"By the way, don't you feel that you have made a hero out of the wrong person? A person breaking up another's marriage [abielulõhkuja], an unfit and careless mother deserting her child [rongaema]. It does not seem to be the best example for young girls." (The translation of the Estonian words is descriptive as no one-word English equivalent exists.)

Ms Laanaru instituted private prosecution proceedings against the applicant for insult by referring to her as "abielulõhkuja" and "rongaema". Before the City Court, the applicant argued that the expressions were intended as a question rather than his opinion, that a question mark had been left out by mistake in editing, that he had no intent to offend, that the expressions were neutral, and that Ms Laanaru's actions justified the question.

By a judgment of 3 April 1997 the Tallinn City Court convicted the applicant of insult under Article 130 of the Criminal Code ("The degradation of another person's honour and dignity in an improper form shall be punished with a fine or detention.") and fined him 220 kroons, ten times the 'daily income' rate. It took note of the expert opinion of the Estonian Language Institute and of the applicant's unwillingness to settle by apologising, and noted that liability did not depend on whether the victim actually possessed the negative qualities ascribed. According to the expert opinion, the words were value judgments expressing a strongly negative and disapproving attitude: "rongaema" indicated a mother who had not cared for her child and "abielulõhkuja" a person who had harmed or broken up someone else's marriage; both phenomena had always been condemned in Estonian society, as reflected in the language, but the words were not linguistically improper.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the context of the whole article had been ignored, that he lacked criminal intent, that the form was not improper, and that the judgment violated his constitutional freedom of speech as a journalist. On 13 May 1997 the Tallinn Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It noted that in private prosecution cases its examination was limited to the offended party's claims, although the whole interview was in the file. While the expressions were not indecent, they were grossly degrading to human dignity and their use abusive in the circumstances; had he stated that she did not raise her child and had destroyed Mr Savisaar's marriage, there would have been no insult. The Constitution and Criminal Code allowed restriction of speech to protect others' reputation and rights, and public figures, despite the press's special interest in them, were entitled to protection of honour and dignity.

The applicant appealed on points of law, arguing that the two words had no Estonian synonyms and that a longer sentence was precluded by objective circumstances of journalism. On 26 August 1997 the Criminal Division of the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal. It held that freedom of speech and of the press under Article 45 of the Constitution and Article 10 ECHR was an essential value but could be restricted to protect honour, good name and the rights of others. It reasoned that civil remedies under section 23(1) of the Law on General Principles of the Civil Code required proof of truth and so were available only for statements of fact; since value judgments could not be proved, a person defamed by a value judgment could in practice only bring a private prosecution under Article 130, as the victim had done. It rejected as groundless the argument that the words were not aimed at Ms Laanaru personally, noting that the applicant's further argument that she was a public figure contradicted it. It observed that there was no legal definition of a public figure in Estonia and that, in Strasbourg case-law, no one had been considered a public figure merely for being a spouse, cohabitant or person close to one; in any event the press's interest in public figures did not mean they could not be offended, and the public had no right to expect their honour to be degraded improperly. Improper form under Article 130 included not only vulgar or indecent words but negative and defamatory figurative expressions; on the basis of the expert opinion, the applicant had publicly treated the victim in a defamatory and improper manner. Journalistic style was free only insofar as it did not degrade human dignity, and the idea could have been expressed in proper Estonian. The absence of synonyms did not justify the expressions, and considerations of newspaper space could not be weighed against human dignity. It lacked competence to revisit the finding that the expressions were a value judgment rather than a question, but noted that insult could also take the form of a question, and that if the newspaper had distorted the applicant's intent by omitting the question mark (as the chief editor's letter of 16 May 1996 suggested), the matter could have been settled by publishing an apology, which the victim had been ready to accept; the refusal of the applicant and the newspaper to do so was further evidence of direct intent to insult.
applicantSubmissions: Article 130 of the Criminal Code, on which the conviction was based, was not formulated with sufficient precision and clarity to satisfy the 'prescribed by law' requirement.
The conviction was not proportionate to the legitimate aim pursued and was not necessary in a democratic society.

The impugned expressions should not have been qualified as insulting; the courts uncritically followed a flawed expert opinion of the Estonian Language Institute which failed to distinguish between the two terms.

The term 'abielulõhkuja' was a statement of fact verifiable by the facts: Ms Laanaru's relationship was with a married man and had actually destroyed his family, as she herself admitted in her memoirs, and the relationship was in the public domain.

The term 'rongaema' was a value judgment; although traditionally carrying a strong negative connotation, in today's pragmatic usage that connotation may have disappeared given radical social changes regarding single motherhood, the interview was aimed at the general public rather than linguists, and even the traditional meaning was not vulgar or insulting; it was based on Ms Laanaru's own reflections on her relationship with her child.
Both expressions were not disproportionate to the underlying facts and should not have been regarded as offensive.

He did not intend to offend Ms Laanaru; the question was meant to provoke a reaction from Mr Russak rather than to state his own opinion, and concerned the attitude of the press towards a particular type of personality in Estonian society rather than Ms Laanaru as an individual.

The dispute was civil in nature and should not have been tried in a criminal court; the Supreme Court wrongly held that honour could be protected against value judgments only through criminal law, a position it reversed on 1 December 1997, and the availability of civil remedies made his criminal conviction a grave injustice.

Ms Laanaru was a public figure in her own right, having held the influential post of counsellor to the Minister of the Interior, been an active social figure and editor, and having placed herself at the centre of the secret tape-recording scandal to gain publicity; she was therefore open to heightened criticism and press scrutiny.
By making her role in Mr Savisaar's first marriage and her relationship with her child a public issue herself, Ms Laanaru lessened the scope of her privacy.

The question pursued a legitimate motive on a matter of public interest, as the tape-recording affair and other controversial measures involving Mr Savisaar while Ms Laanaru was his counsellor raised legitimate questions about the ethics and values of those in power; the expressions served the public interest in receiving information and not mere curiosity.

He did not exceed the limits of acceptable criticism, his journalistic freedom outweighed Ms Laanaru's right to respect for private and family life, and the courts' decisions amounted to a form of censure likely to discourage journalists from similar criticism in the future.
governmentSubmissions: Article 130 of the Criminal Code defined the offence of insult in sufficiently precise terms to allow the applicant to regulate his professional conduct, and its interpretation by the domestic courts did not go beyond what was reasonably foreseeable.
The interference pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the reputation or rights of others.
The interference corresponded to a pressing social need, was proportionate, was supported by relevant and sufficient reasons, and remained within the national margin of appreciation.

The wider limits of criticism applicable to politicians and civil servants did not apply to Ms Laanaru to the same extent, as she was active in politics only as Mr Savisaar's wife, collaborator and supporter, not independently; references to the private life of an ordinary citizen, even one linked to a prominent politician, did not concern a matter of serious public interest.

The relationship between a woman who had left the civil service and a man who had at the time withdrawn from politics was a very private matter, and insulting comments on a private person's family life served no social purpose.

The applicant chose the words to provoke and create sensational headlines and did not act in good faith; in any event an alleged need to inform the public could not exonerate him from respecting journalistic ethics and defamation law.

The applicant was not convicted for describing facts or expressing critical opinion about Ms Laanaru's personality or private life, but for his choice of insulting words; describing her as having broken up a marriage or not caring for her child would not have been an insult, as the Court of Appeal pointed out.
The words 'rongaema' and 'abielulõhkuja' have a very special meaning in Estonian with no English equivalent, and their specific linguistic and cultural nature must be taken into account.
The words were used to denigrate Ms Laanaru in public opinion rather than to describe known aspects of her life; entrusting a child to grandparents is quite common in Estonia.

Ms Laanaru had not placed her private life in the public domain: the interview was with another journalist, not her, and she had obtained a court order on 29 March 1996 preventing publication of her memoirs, no longer intending to make them public.

The proceedings were a private prosecution initiated by Ms Laanaru; the City Court attempted a settlement which the applicant refused by declining to apologise, the public prosecutor never intervened despite being invited, and the executive remained entirely neutral.
The sanction was only a modest fine of 220 kroons, ten times the minimum daily salary.

The domestic courts balanced the Article 8 rights of Ms Laanaru against the applicant's Article 10 rights, and the Supreme Court applied the same test as the Strasbourg Court with ample reference to its case-law in a thoroughly reasoned judgment.
